analysis.one_liner: Imposes cost-benefit, hearing, and court-review hurdles that make major federal regulations harder to issue.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the federal rulemaking process that agencies use to turn laws into regulations. For any rule with a large economic impact, agencies would have to prove the rule maximizes net benefits, defend it at formal hearings where regulated parties can cross-examine them and the agency bears the burden of proof, clear a political review office before even publishing a proposal, and survive broader court challenges. The bill also includes some transparency measures, such as putting the studies behind a rule into a public docket and giving people more time to comment.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — energy, manufacturing, chemicals, finance, and others facing costly federal rules — gain the most. Every new requirement gives them another point to delay, narrow, or defeat a rule they dislike, and the expanded judicial review makes court challenges easier to win.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to adopt the rule alternative that maximizes net benefits, and could choose a different rule only if the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs approves and the agency justifies the unquantified costs and benefits [S2][S3].

For 'high-impact' rules — those with an annual economic effect of $500 million or more — any interested party could petition for a formal public hearing with oral presentations and cross-examination, with the burden of proof on the agency proposing the rule [S2][S3].

Agencies could not publish a proposed major rule until the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs finishes reviewing it, and the bill expands the scope of judicial review, including requiring courts to check that the factual findings behind high-impact rules are supported by substantial evidence [S2][S3].

The bill also adds public-facing transparency: all studies and models behind a rule must go into a public docket, comment periods would run at least 60 days (90 for major rules) plus a 30-day response window, and agencies would be barred from lobbying the public for or against their own proposed rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public pays through slower and weaker federal protections. Rules on air and water pollution, workplace safety, consumer product safety, and financial practices are typically 'major' rules, so each would face more hearings, more paperwork, more political review, and more lawsuits before it could take effect — and some would never get there.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public relying on federal protections

drawbacks.text: Requiring agencies to adopt the net-benefit-maximizing alternative, with exceptions gated by a political appointee at OIRA, would tie agencies' hands on protections whose benefits are real but hard to price, such as preventing illness or protecting civil rights [S3].

Formal hearings with cross-examination and the burden of proof on the agency would turn writing a high-impact rule into litigation, stretching rulemakings out for years and raising the odds that contested rules simply are not issued [S3].

The expanded judicial review would invite more lawsuits against rules, shifting even more of the policy fight into courtrooms where well-funded regulated parties have the advantage of time and money [S3].

To be fair, the transparency provisions are real improvements: public dockets, longer comment windows, and a ban on agencies pitching their own rules to the public would make rulemaking more visible to ordinary citizens, not just organized interests [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency pieces are genuine but modest; the core of the bill is a set of hurdles that would make the biggest public protections — the rules with the largest economic impact — the hardest to issue and the easiest to kill. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill's main measurable effect would be fewer, slower, and weaker major regulations, and that the parties best positioned to use the new hearings, petitions, and lawsuits are the regulated companies themselves, not ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never received a single cosponsor, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Beth Van Duyne (R-TX) introduced the bill on January 20, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
No member of the House from either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The House Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies keep today's rulemaking procedures, and the industries that would have used the new hearings, petitions, and lawsuits to fight major rules did not get that tool. The public's existing environmental, workplace, and consumer protections were left untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public; regulated industries lost nothing but gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Beth Van Duyne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and not one member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the outcome was decided by committee inaction rather than a party split.

industries.note: The bill would make the largest rules — environmental, workplace, consumer, and financial — the hardest to issue and easiest to challenge, which is worth a great deal to the companies they cover. The industry's gain here comes directly at the cost of the protections ordinary people rely on.

industries.industry: Law firms and consultancies specializing in federal rules
industries.note: Formal hearings, hearing petitions, and expanded court review would create years of new challenge work on every major rule. Some of that work (public comment, petitions) is also open to ordinary citizens, but well-funded companies can use it far more effectively.
